discovery: Invention and development of the optical lattice clock

nominees.name: Hidetoshi Katori
nominees.affiliation: University of Tokyo and RIKEN, Japan

nominees.name: Jun Ye
nominees.affiliation: JILA, NIST and University of Colorado Boulder, USA

subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics / precision measurement
motivation: Katori conceived the optical lattice clock and the 'magic wavelength' trapping that cancels light shifts, allowing thousands of neutral atoms to be interrogated at once without perturbing their clock transition. Ye turned this idea into the world's most precise and accurate clocks, reaching fractional uncertainties near 10^-18 and below, and pioneered many-body and spin-squeezing techniques in lattice clocks. Together they improved timekeeping by more than two orders of magnitude over caesium standards. These clocks now resolve gravitational redshift over millimetre height differences, perform relativistic geodesy, set the tightest laboratory limits on drifts of fundamental constants and on ultralight dark matter, and underpin the coming redefinition of the SI second. This is precision measurement at its finest: decades of instrumental ingenuity that turned a technique into a discovery tool for fundamental physics.
